title: Chapter Map
notes: Start with the chapter's architecture, using the introduction on printed pages 51-52 as orientation. The lecture moves from Definition 2.1 style local chart data to global objects that charts can carry: vector bundles, divisors, projective linear systems, blow-ups, and finally the differential calculus of types. Tell students that every later construction asks the same question: what local holomorphic data survives a change of chart?

title: Holomorphic Atlases
notes: Use the overlap picture to slow down Definition 2.1 from Section 2.1, printed pages 52-65. The underlying space has the size of a real manifold of dimension 2n, but the admissible coordinates are complex n-tuples. The content is in the transition maps: once z_j composed with z_i inverse is holomorphic on every overlap, holomorphic functions, tangent vectors, and later forms can be tested locally and glued consistently.

title: Compact Rigidity
notes: After the definition, emphasize the first global shock in Section 2.1: compact connected complex manifolds have no nonconstant holomorphic functions to the affine line. This is just the maximum principle seen globally, but it explains why the chapter immediately cares about meromorphic functions. The algebraic dimension is introduced as a measurement of the meromorphic function field, and it separates compact complex manifolds that look algebraic from those with too few meromorphic coordinates.

title: Example Zoo
notes: Section 2.1 gives examples to prevent the definition from feeling empty. Contrast affine space, projective space, complex tori, hypersurfaces, quotients, and Grassmannians. The torus polygon borrows the visual language of the topology catalog but is drawn here as a fresh SVG. The teaching point is that local holomorphic charts do not decide projectivity; projectivity requires enough line bundles and sections, a theme that returns in Sections 2.3 and 2.4.

title: Submanifolds And Subvarieties
notes: When Section 2.1 discusses submanifolds and analytic subvarieties, separate the smooth local coordinate theorem from the broader equation-cut-out viewpoint. A complex submanifold can be made into a coordinate plane after choosing suitable holomorphic coordinates. An analytic subvariety is more flexible and is tracked by an ideal sheaf, hence the exact sequence displayed here, but it may have singular points where the coordinate-plane picture breaks.

title: Holomorphic Vector Bundles
notes: Section 2.2, printed pages 66-76, begins with the local trivialization definition. Make students say aloud what is local and what is global: locally the bundle is just a product with C to the r, but on overlaps the fiber coordinates are transformed by holomorphic GL(r,C)-valued functions. The displayed cocycle relation is the whole gluing law. It is also the template for line bundles, tangent bundles, normal bundles, and later sheaf cohomology descriptions.

title: Bundle Operations
notes: The operations in Section 2.2 are not separate mysteries; they are functorial operations on the transition matrices. If the original changes of frame are holomorphic, then block sums, tensor products, exterior powers, symmetric powers, duals, determinants, and pullbacks are holomorphic as well. This viewpoint is efficient because the same local calculation will later give the tangent bundle, canonical bundle, normal bundle, and line bundles associated with divisors.

title: Tautological Bundles
notes: Use projective space to make line bundles concrete before discussing the Picard group. The tautological bundle O(-1) over projective space has fiber equal to the actual line represented by the point [v], and O(1) is its dual. Section 2.2 introduces Pic(X), the exponential sequence, and the first Chern class as a bridge from holomorphic transition functions to topological cohomology classes. The point is not to compute every Picard group yet, but to see line bundles as measurable objects.

title: Tangent Normal Canonical
notes: The tangent bundle is the first nontrivial vector bundle that every complex manifold owns. Its transition matrices are Jacobians of holomorphic coordinate changes, so the bundle is holomorphic. From there, Section 2.2 introduces the normal bundle of a submanifold, the canonical bundle of holomorphic top forms, adjunction, and the Kodaira dimension. Present these as one family: tangent data, quotient normal directions, and determinant duals of tangent data.

title: Divisor Ledger
notes: Section 2.3, printed pages 77-90, turns meromorphic behavior into bookkeeping. A divisor records codimension-one zero and pole orders, with effective divisors having only nonnegative entries and principal divisors coming from a meromorphic function. The map from Div(X) to Pic(X) sends D to O(D). Explain that the line bundle remembers how local equations for the divisor change from chart to chart, while principal divisors disappear because a global meromorphic function supplies the trivialization.

title: Sections To Projective Maps
notes: Continue Section 2.3 by linking divisors to maps. A nonzero section of a line bundle has a zero divisor, and a collection of sections gives projective coordinates whenever there is no base point. The formula is familiar, but the point is subtle: the values s_i(x) live in the same one-dimensional fiber L_x, so their ratios are well-defined after choosing any local trivialization. This prepares the projective-space computations and the definition of ampleness.

title: Projective Space Calculus
notes: Section 2.4, printed pages 91-97, is the computational heart of projective space. Global sections of O(k) are homogeneous polynomials of degree k, while negative twists have no nonzero global sections. The Euler sequence packages the tangent bundle in terms of O and O(1), and taking determinants gives K of projective n-space as O minus n minus one. These formulas are not decorative; the next slide uses them immediately in adjunction for hypersurfaces.

title: Hypersurface Adjunction
notes: Now put the projective formulas to work. A smooth hypersurface defined by a homogeneous polynomial of degree d has normal bundle O_X(d), because the defining equation changes as a section of O(d). Combining this with K of projective space and adjunction gives K_X equal to O_X(d-n-1). This one line explains why quadrics, cubics, quintics, and higher-degree hypersurfaces land in very different birational worlds.

title: Blow-Ups
notes: Section 2.5, printed pages 98-103, introduces blow-ups as a controlled surgery. Away from the center Y nothing changes. Over Y, the space remembers not just the point but the limiting normal direction, so the exceptional divisor is the projectivized normal bundle P(N_{Y/X}). Mention the canonical shift for a smooth center of codimension r, because it signals that blow-ups change birational geometry while leaving the complement of the center untouched.

title: Almost Complex To Dolbeault
notes: Section 2.6, printed pages 104-112, brings the chapter back to differential calculus. An almost complex structure is a real endomorphism squaring to minus the identity, so the complexified tangent bundle has plus i and minus i eigenspaces. Integrability, by Newlander-Nirenberg, is the condition that these data come from holomorphic charts. Once integrable, differential forms split into (p,q)-types, d decomposes into partial plus dbar, and Dolbeault cohomology records the dbar complex.

title: Synthesis Exercise
notes: Close by making students connect the chapter's three languages without adding new definitions. First, divisors give line bundles, line bundles have sections, and basepoint-free sections produce projective maps. Second, holomorphic charts give an integrable almost complex structure and hence the Dolbeault splitting; Newlander-Nirenberg runs the logic back. Third, blow-ups replace a smooth center by an exceptional divisor of normal directions while preserving the complement. These are the tools the next chapter will use on Kahler manifolds.
